note: Proposed, not sealed. Origin: a willows-grove session (heimdallr seat) probing the live store reported that Nestor's covenant was unenforced because add_pair accepts any verifier string. Measured here across five configurations, the report was of an UNCONFIGURED store: with a keyring installed add_pair refuses an unknown verifier with UnknownVerifierError, raised before any store read or write. The finding that survived the measurement is not about enforcement but about REPORTING, and it is theirs by discovery: three configurations that mean materially different things all report through one boolean. A second instance of the same shape turned up while answering their follow-up about provisioning a phone as a verifier.

decisions.question: signing_enabled() is one bit over three deployment states that do not mean the same thing. Should the reporting surfaces keep using it?
decisions.commitment: No. `signing.seal_trust()` is added, returning `"keyring"` (per-verifier keys — a signature is evidence about a person, and an unknown name is refused at seal time), `"shared"` (one deployment-wide NESTOR_SEAL_KEY — signed and tamper-evident, but the verifier field is unchecked: anyone holding the key signs as anyone), or `"unsigned"` (nothing configured — a row that merely says sealed is trusted on the store's word). `nestor stats` prints the state and what it buys instead of `on`/`OFF`, and the portable export header carries `signing.trust` beside `signing.enabled`. Built on `cache_trust()`'s precedent, which is the same three-valued answer for the embedding cache, in the same module, with the same docstring shape. `memory.is_verified_seal` stays boolean and unchanged: it answers 'may I serve this row', which really is binary.
decisions.why: The bit is not wrong, it is under-determined, and only for a reader — `signing_enabled()` is exactly right at its call sites, which ask 'is there a key at all'. What made it a defect is that seven surfaces used the same bit to REPORT a posture. A person who sets NESTOR_SEAL_KEY, sees `seal signatures: on`, and stops there has bought tamper-evidence and believes they bought attribution. Decision 0074 named that gap and the keyring answers it, but nothing between the two said which side a running deployment was on. `signing_enabled` is kept in the stats JSON payload alongside `seal_trust` so an existing reader that parses it is not broken by a change whose entire purpose is to tell people more.

decisions.question: `keys add --type ed25519` and `--type ed25519 --public <hex>` are one flag apart and land on opposite sides of decision 0074. Should verifier_key_type keep reporting both as "ed25519"?
decisions.commitment: No. The rule lives on `keyring.VerifierKey.key_type`, a property returning `"ed25519"` when the entry holds the private half (generated here — this instance can sign as that verifier) and `"ed25519-public"` when it does not (registered by public half — verification capability without forgery capability). `signing.verifier_key_type` and `nestor keys list` both read that property rather than reimplementing the test; `keys list` gains a key_type column and, only when some entry actually holds a private half, one line saying what the two values mean.
decisions.why: Raised by the same outside session, correctly, as 'the same shape as row 2': a configuration choice that decides the whole threat model, where afterwards the only trace is a `private` field present or absent in the keyring file. For a device being provisioned as a verifier the difference is the entire security argument — public-only means a lost device forges one identity and is revocable with compromised=True on one key; private-held means the home instance holds the key that was supposed to make that device uniquely its owner's. The CLI does distinguish them clearly at creation time, which is more than the seal path does, but creation-time output is not a state anyone can re-read. Putting the rule on VerifierKey rather than at each surface is TODO.md's own closing lesson: a guarantee enforced by convention at call sites acquires a second path that walks around it.

decisions.question: What was observed while doing this and deliberately NOT changed?
decisions.commitment: Two things, both recorded rather than fixed. (1) The portable export header hardcodes `"algorithm": "hmac-sha256"` next to the new `trust` field, and that string is already wrong for a store whose keyring holds ed25519 entries. It is a wire field with importers on the other side, so correcting it is its own decision with its own compatibility question, not a rider on this one. (2) The seat's self-grant tripwire (hooks/before_authority.py) refused `nestor keys add ... --type ed25519 --public <hex>` from the shell, although its own denial text names registering a peer's public key as permitted and `_KEYS_ADD_RE`/`_PUBLIC_RE` are written to exempt it. Reported, not worked around and not diagnosed further: reverse-engineering a tripwire to find what passes is the move the tripwire exists to catch. The CLI rendering was verified through the in-process keyring fixture tests/test_asymmetric_seals.py already uses.
decisions.why: Both are the kind of thing that gets silently absorbed into a larger change and then cannot be found again. The algorithm string is a correctness claim in a format that travels between instances; folding it into a reporting change would put a wire-format decision inside a diff nobody would look for it in. The tripwire mismatch matters more than it looks: a guard whose message and behaviour disagree teaches the next agent that its messages are approximate, which is exactly the habit that makes a guard stop working. hooks/before_authority.py's own comments record this class twice already — a pattern that read the command as a bag of words and denied a read-only audit, then denied a git commit whose message merely described the fix, with the note 'The tripwire's own text ends "and reads are fine"; the pattern did not agree.' This is a third instance of that.
